The ORP of a solution is defined as the tendency of the solution to gain or lose electron.(Rittmann and McCarty, 2001) A solution with a positive ORP is characterized by oxidizing conditions (higher tendency to gain electron, e.g., ½ O2 + 2H+ + 2e- = H2O), whereas a solution with negative ORP value represents  a reducing environment (higher tendency to lose electron, e.g., H2 = 2H+ + 2e-). The oxidation and reduction half-reactions always occur simultaneously to result in a combined reaction (e.g., ½ O2 + H2 = H2O). The ORP was originally measured with a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) as reference half-cell (Eh). However, the application of ORP electrode with a Ag/AgCl reference electrode (EAg) has gained popularity due to ease of operation and maintenance.(Cole-Parmer, 2018) The correlation between these two types of electrodes according to the manufacturer (Cole Parmer, USA) is: EAg = Eh + 200 mV(at 35 oC). The ORP value is affected by temperature and pH according to the manufacturer and confirmed with experiments of measuring ORP at different temperatures (10 to 50 oC, n = 9) and different pH buffers (pH 4, 7 and 10, n = 9). The effects are presented as: ORP (mV-EAg) = -1.32 Temperature (oC) + 264, R² = 0.999 and ORP (mV-EAg) = -57.33 pH + 410, R² = 0.999.

ORP, due to its high sensitivity towards the dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration (ORP has a linear correlation with the natural logarithm (ln) of the DO concentration, Figure S1), was selected as the control parameter for micro-aeration in this research. A typical DO probe has a detection range of 0.1 to 10 mg/L with accuracy of 0.1- 0.2 mg/L, while an ORP probe operates within the range of -2,000 to 2,000 mV.(Cole-Parmer, 2018) According to the correlation between DO and ORP, a DO of 0.1 mg/L is equivalent to an ORP of -96 mV (Figure S1). Even though the correlation range is limited due to the DO probe detection limit (0.1 to 10 mg/L), a DO of less than 0.1 mg/L is likely to follow this exponential correlation trend line and could be predicted using the measured ORP value. Therefore, it can be estimated that anaerobic conditions with an ORP of -495 mV (Figure 2E) have an equivalent DO of 1.15 x 10-8 mg/L (or 0.36 x 10-3 nM O2); and a 25 mV increase in ORP under micro-aerobic condition is equivalent to a DO increase of 1.98 x 10-8 mg/L (or 0.62 x 10-3 nM O2).

When oxygen is supplied to an anaerobic process, it is consumed by the reducing equivalents available, resulting in a rise in the ORP. In other words, the extent of the change in ORP depends on the relative abundance of the electron acceptor (e.g., O2, NAD+) and reducing equivalents (e.g., NADH) that subsequently influence the intracellular metabolism of the microbial populations. The redox potential difference between anaerobic and micro-aerobic conditions was reported to be +25mV (Khanal and Huang, 2006; Krayzelova et al., 2014), +35mV (Jenicek et al., 2011) and +50 to +100 mV(Khanal and Huang, 2003), with more positive values under micro-aerobic conditions. Thus, micro-aeration at a target ORP of >25 mV above the baseline ORP (anaerobic condition) was expected to provide micro-aerobic conditions in the bioreactor. In this research, micro-aerobic conditions were maintained via ORP-controlled intermittent micro-aeration (24-h on and 24-h off)  at a target ORP of -470 mV, which was 25 mV above the baseline ORP of an anaerobic bioreactor, following the control scheme previously reported.(Khanal and Huang, 2003) When the ORP of the reactor reached 10 mV below the target value, the ORP controller triggered the solenoid valve (DVP-2DC1D, Automation Direct, GA, USA) to inject oxygen into the bottom of the reactor via a 2-mm inner diameter stainless steel tube. The injected oxygen promptly spiked up the ORP to approximately 10 mV above the target value, which then prompted the solenoid valve to close thereby stopping the micro-aeration. The ORP then gradually reduced until it reached below the set point, which started the next cycle of micro-aeration. Hence, a uniform ORP profile oscillating between 10 mV below and 10 mV above the target ORP was obtained as shown in Figure S2.

Besides the above mentioned ORP control strategy (24-h intermittent ORP-controlled micro-aeration at ORP setpoint = baseline + 25 mV), two independent sets of experiments with different ORP control strategies were conducted with results shown in Table S6. Both continuous ORP control at baseline ORP + 25 mV and 24-h intermittent (every other day) ORP control at baseline ORP + 50 mV showed adverse effects on reactor performance (increased VFA concentration and reduced methane yield, Table S5).

The pH was measured daily using a pH meter (Accumet AB15, Fisher, OH, USA). ORP was measured on-line using an ORP probe with Pt electrode and Ag/AgCl reference electrode filled with 3-M KCl (EW-27003-40, Cole-Parmer, IL, USA). All ORP or redox potential values in this study were reported in mV with Ag/AgCl as a reference electrode (EAg). The standard redox potential value (Eh) with standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) at 35 oC can be calculated according to the manufacturer’s guidelines using the following expression: Eh = EAg – 200 mV.

Daily biogas production was collected in a 10-L Tedlar gas bag (CEL Scientific Corporation, CA, USA) and quantified using a milli-gas counter (Ritter US LLC, NY, USA). Gas volumes were normalized to standard temperature (0 oC or 273 K) and pressure (1 atm) and reported as NmL. Biogas composition (i.e., CH4, CO2, N2, H2 and O2) was determined using gas chromatography equipped with thermal conductivity detector (GC-TCD) at 80 oC (GC2014, Shimadzu, Japan) using a packed column (80/100 Hayesep D column, 2 m x 2.1 mm ID, Supelco, PA, USA). The column temperature was programmed at 80 oC and held for 40 min. Daily methane yield was calculated and reported as NmL CH4/g VS added.

Total VFA-to-total alkalinity (VFA/ALK) ratio was analyzed every two days using an autotitrator (TitraLab AT1000, Hach, Germany) with FOS/TAC software (HACH, Germany) based on the method of (Kafle et al., 2012). The VFA/ALK ratio was reported as a mass ratio of acetic acid  (HAc) equivalent over CaCO3 equivalent. The total VFA values from the autotitrator were reported as g/L as acetic acid (HAc) equivalent and were not statistically different (p > 0.05) with the values obtained by adding the concentrations of individual VFA.

Individual VFAs (acetic, propionic, butyric, iso-butyric, valeric, and iso-valeric acids) were determined every two days using gas chromatography equipped with flame-ionization detector (GC-FID) (GC2014, Shimadzu, Japan) using a capillary column (ZB-Wax Plus column, 30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 μm, Phenomenex, CA, USA). Helium was used as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 2 mL/min. The temperature was programmed to increase from 50 oC to 180 oC at a rate of 20 oC/min, and held for 10 min, the split ratio was 20, the purge flow was 1 mL/min, and injector and detector temperatures were 250 oC each. The samples for individual VFA analyses were prepared as previously described.3 TS and VS were analyzed following Standard Methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 2005). Fiber compositions (e.g., hemicellulose, cellulose, and acid insoluble lignin) were analyzed using a cell wall fractionation method(Faithfull, 2002) using the Fiber Analyzer (ANKOM 200, ANKOM, NY, USA).

For the carbon mass balance analysis (Figure 3), the carbon contents of influent and effluent samples were obtained from total carbon content (g C/g TS) analysis at Agricultural Diagnostic Service Center, University of Hawaii at Manoa; data of CH4 and CO2 were converted to g C from gas production at standard temperature and pressure (273 K and 1 atm) using ideal gas law equation PV = nRT; data of “Biomass & Intermediates” representing unmeasured components were calculated from influent carbon (4.88 g C/day at OLR 5.0 g VS/L/day) minus carbon content from other components. Samples for carbon mass balance were collected on three consecutive days during anaerobic and micro-aerobic conditions of three replicate experiments (Anaerobic condition: days 114-116 of Replicate 1, days 164-166 of Replicate 2, days 83-85 of Replicate 3; Micro-aerobic condition: days 153-155 of Replicate 1, days 214-216 of Replicate 2, days 108-110 of Replicate 3). Data from days after bicarbonate addition were avoided to minimize interference to biogas composition.

Triplicate experiments were conducted with a total of 250 observations at standard conditions (1 atm, 25 oC, pH 7.0) with the effluent of the reactor operated at an OLR 5.0 g VS/L/day from a stable period (days 80 to 83 of Replicate 1). The effluent was filtered through GF/C paper to eliminate microbial oxygen consumption. The experiment was conducted in a 120-mL gas-tight bottle filled with 100 mL of prepared effluent. The bottle was flushed with N2 gas for 5 min to create anaerobic conditions (the DO reached its limit of detection of 0.1 mg/L). Air was then slowly injected into the bottle using a glass syringe to increase the DO from 0.1 to 10 mg/L, while ORP and DO probes (Cole Parmer, USA) were simultaneously used to monitor and record values every 5 s.

Figure S2: ORP profile of bioreactor under uncontrolled ORP and ORP-controlled micro-aeration for Replicate 1: daily average ORP of uncontrolled ORP (open circles) and controlled ORP (closed circles) (A); ORP profile at micro-aerobic condition for three days (B); ORP profile at micro-aerobic condition for one day with data recorded every 10 min, ORP controller setpoint: value at which solenoid valve open to start injecting oxygen, average ORP setpoint: target ORP value (C); micro-aeration intensity over time (D).

Figure S3: Reactor instability and recovery by micro-aeration at an OLR of 5.0 g VS/L/day for Replicate 2 (days 137 to 216). Process performance in terms of pH and VFA/ALK ratio with vertical lines indicating additions of NaHCO3 to control pH (A); total VFA and methane yield (B); individual VFA concentrations (iso-butyric, valeric, and iso-valeric acid concentrations were below 0.2 g L-1 at all times and are not shown) (C); biogas composition (D); and daily average ORP of uncontrolled ORP (open circles) and controlled ORP every other day at ORP set point (SP) of -450 mV (black closed circles) and -425 mV (gray closed circle) (E). The mean (± standard deviation) uncontrolled ORP during anaerobic period from days 137 to 176 was calculated to be -475 ± 15 mV. The mean controlled ORP with set point of -450 mV (black closed circles: days 177 to 193 and 209 to 216) was -449 ± 7 mV. The mean controlled ORP with set point of -425 mV (gray closed circles: days 194 to 208) was -426 ± 6 mV. Since micro-aeration was performed every other day, the uncontrolled ORP values (open circles) reported after day 177 represent the daily average ORP on the days without micro-aeration (the mean from days 177 to 216 was calculated to be -466 ± 11 mV). Orange arrows in the x-axis indicate the days that biomass samples were taken for microbial community analysis (days 150 and 192).

Figure S4: Reactor instability and recovery by micro-aeration at an OLR of 5.0 g VS/L/day for Replicate 3 (days 46 to 125). Process performance in terms of pH and VFA/ALK ratio with vertical lines indicating additions of NaHCO3 to control pH (A); total VFA and methane yield (B); individual VFA concentration (iso-butyric, valeric, and iso-valeric acid concentrations were below 0.2 g/L at all times and are not shown) (C); biogas composition (D); and daily average ORP of uncontrolled ORP (open circles) and controlled ORP every other day (closed circles) (E). The mean (± standard deviation) uncontrolled ORP from days 46 to 85 was calculated to be -500 ± 20 mV. The mean of controlled ORP (-475 ± 3 mV) was the average of ORP values of days with ORP-based micro-aeration (closed circles) from days 86 to 110. Since micro-aeration was performed every other day, the mean of uncontrolled ORP values (open circles) from days 86 to 110 was -497 ± 5 mV, representing the daily average ORP on the days without micro-aeration. The mean value of uncontrolled ORP after micro-aeration period (days 111 to 125) was -508 ± 3 mV. Orange arrows in the x-axis indicate the days that biomass samples were taken for microbial community analysis (days 64 and 108).
